note_on_method: Two kinds of claim appear below and they are kept apart deliberately. Claims about the world - how many courts a park has, what it costs, when it is busy - come from the Cities of Scottsdale and Mesa and are cited. Claims about our own coverage are facts about this dataset rather than about Maricopa County, and are worded so a reader cannot mistake one for the other. Maricopa is by some distance the largest county this directory has published in, and two cities of it are on this page.

slots.coverage: Two cities in Maricopa County are published here: Scottsdale, with four venues and twenty-nine courts, and Mesa, with three venues and twenty-six courts. Fifty-five courts in total, every one of them verified against the operating City's own pages. Maricopa County also contains Phoenix, Chandler, Glendale, Gilbert, Tempe, Peoria, Surprise, Goodyear and Avondale - some four and a half million people, and on any reasonable estimate several hundred public pickleball courts - and none of those cities has been checked against a named source, so none appears anywhere on this site. Two locations inside the published cities are also absent and named on their city pages: Scottsdale Community College, whose six lighted courts host a free City-run public programme at an address the geocoder places in no incorporated place at all, and six Mesa parks that print the words "Pickleball Court" without ever printing a number.
slots.distribution: The two published cities are documented in opposite ways, and the contrast is the most useful thing on this page. Scottsdale's twenty-nine courts are spread evenly across four parks in the north and east of the city - ten at Horizon Park, eight at Cholla Park, eight at Ashler Hills Park and three at Thompson Peak Park. Every one of the four is lit, three of the four are confirmed free, and all of them run from sunrise until 10:30 p.m. Mesa is the reverse shape: of its twenty-six courts, twenty-one sit at a single address. The Mesa Tennis & Pickleball Center is a staffed, ticketed facility with a pro shop where a court costs $9.00 an hour before 5 p.m. and $13.00 after, and the city's other two published venues are a four-court allocation at Kleinman Park and one shared, netless court at Chaparral Park. So the county's largest single concentration of verified courts is also the only one you have to pay for. What the two cities share is lighting: forty-nine of the fifty-five courts here are confirmed lit, which in a county where the summer daytime is unusable for outdoor sport is the whole of what makes them a usable inventory.
slots.gaps: This page carried a prediction until recently and the prediction was wrong, which is worth recording rather than quietly deleting. It said a second Maricopa city would be unusually hard to add, because Gilbert, Mesa and Tucson had all refused our fetcher outright and Chandler's parks pages did not resolve where expected. Mesa is now the second city, and it was not hard: retested, www.mesaaz.gov answered a plain request with no special handling at all. Whatever refused us before was a fact about one day rather than a property of the operator, and the same turned out to be true of Durham in North Carolina. The remaining gap is still large and still real - Phoenix, Chandler, Glendale, Gilbert and Tempe are unread, and Phoenix publishes a county-wide court layer that records one row per court with no address and no count, which is the shape of data this site refuses to add up. Nothing outside a municipal parks department appears here at all: no clubs, resorts, HOAs or commercial venues in the county carry a source we could read, which in a retirement-and-resort county is a large and specific hole.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there in Maricopa County?
faqs.a: We do not know, and no honest page can tell you. Maricopa is the fourth most populous county in the United States and includes Phoenix, Chandler, Glendale, Gilbert and Tempe as well as the two cities here. What we have checked is 55 courts across seven venues - 29 in Scottsdale and 26 in Mesa - each with a source and a date you can see.

faqs.q: Why are only Scottsdale and Mesa listed?
faqs.a: Because they are the only municipalities in the county whose courts we have confirmed against a named source. A city appears here once three or more of its venues carry a source_url and a date_checked. Phoenix, Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale and Tempe have not been read. Mesa itself was refused on an earlier pass because its site turned our fetcher away; on retesting it did not, which is why it is here now.

An unusually complete page. The City publishes each venue's court count, address, lighting and hours together, and each park's own page adds the price and the rule for sharing a court — standard game to 11, win by two, a 30-minute limit, then rotate off for waiting players. It is the only operator in this directory that publishes court etiquette, and the only one that states when its courts are busiest.

faqs.q: Are the courts on this page free?
faqs.a: In Scottsdale, mostly: three of its four venues state "They are free to use" on their own park pages. In Mesa, no. The Tennis & Pickleball Center charges $9.00 per court per hour before 5 p.m. and $13.00 after, and Mesa publishes no price at all for its other two venues - which is not the same as publishing that they are free, so this site does not call them free.

faqs.q: How often is this checked again?
faqs.a: These pages were read on 4 September 2026 and each one is snapshotted into the repository that builds this site, then re-asserted on every build. One of the four venues, Thompson Peak Park, was closed for resurfacing at the time of checking — our build will fail when the City removes that notice, which is how a closure on this site stops being true rather than quietly persisting.

faqs.q: Which Maricopa city is likely next?
faqs.a: Whichever one publishes its court counts on a page we can read and re-check. That is the only test, and volume is a tiebreak rather than a qualification: a city with four documented venues beats a city with forty undocumented ones. Phoenix is the largest unread city and the least promising on current evidence - its own court layer holds one row per court with no address and no count, and counting those rows to reach a total is a derivation this site has refused before. Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale and Tempe are simply unread.
